Every Thanksgiving, Americans gather around tables filled with familiar traditions. Turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, and pumpkin pie represent far more than a holiday meal. They represent family, gratitude, and the comfort of being together.

But this year, those traditions come with a higher price tag.

According to the American Farm Bureau Federation’s 2026 Thanksgiving dinner[survey](https://www.fb.org/intel/markets/thanksgiving-dinner-cost-ticks-upward-in-2026?ref=foodsafetynews.com)**,**the average cost of a traditional meal for 10 people has climbed to $58.63, an increase of approximately 6 percent over last year. A 16-pound frozen turkey now averages $23.68, roughly 10 percent more than in 2025.

For economists, these figures offer another measure of inflation, supply-chain pressures, and changing market conditions. For families, however, they represent something much more personal.

And for those of us who have spent decades working to prevent foodborne illness, they raise an uncomfortable question:

When food becomes more expensive, are families more likely to take risks with its safety?

**The decisions behind the dinner**  
Food safety is often presented as a matter of knowledge and individual responsibility. Cook poultry to 165 degrees F. Refrigerate perishable foods within two hours. Avoid cross-contamination. Store leftovers properly.

These are essential practices, supported by decades of public health research.
